full_judgment:
(a) In Writ Petition No.5198 of 2003, the property in question was acquired vide LA Case No. 10 of 1963-64 as per the provisions of section 93A of the Town Improvement Act, 1953. The Government vide the impugned gazette notification withdraw 14-68 acres of land from acquisition exercising the power conferred under section 8(b) of the Emergency Acquisition of Property Act 1948. The case of the petitioner is that the authority cannot publish such gazette notification exercising the power conferred under section 8(b) of the Act of 1948 as the same was already repealed with effect from 13-3-1982 and being aggrieved moved this Writ Petitions and obtained the present rule. 

 (b) In Writ Petition No. 11817 of 2006, 11818 of 2006, 11819 of 2006 and 3466 of 2007 the respective petitioners on an advertisement made by RAJUK applied for allotment of plots. On the basis of their applications the RAJUK issued formal allotment letters in their favour. Pursuant to the allotment letters the respective petitioners paid in full the royalty/premium to the lessor namely RAJUK and after satisfaction the lessor namely RAJUK executed registered lease deeds for 99 years of the respective plots as mentioned in these Writ Petition with the petitioner and also handed over formal possession thereon. The further case of the petitioners is that they have constructed house as per approved plan and enjoying the possession thereon. All on a sudden, some people entered into the premises and claimed ownership of the said plots by virtue of sale deeds obtained from the original owners from whom the aforesaid land was acquired by the lessor as per Town Improvement Act of 1953 (hereinafter referred as Act of 1953). On query the petitioners came to know that the Ministry of Land issued a gazette notification which is impugned in all these Writ Petitioners wherein the Ministry of Land released certain portion of land from acquisition exercising the Power conferred under section 8(b) of the Act of 1948. 

 6. In Writ Petition Nos. 11817 to 11819 of 2006 and 3466 of 2007 Mr Khalilur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners adopted the submission made by the Mr Khan Saifur Rahman, the learned Senior counsel appearing in Writ Petitioner No. 5198 of 2003. In addition to the said submission he further submits that the property was acquired under the Act of 1953 which is a separate law, thus the Act of 1948 has no manner of application in the case of any Acquisition and Requisition made under the Act of 1953. He submits that section 8(b) o f the Act of 1948 only empowers the government to withdraw from Acquisition of any land which has been acquired as per section 5 of the Act of 1948 and also before payment of any compensation. He submits that from the plain reading sections 79, 101 and other provisions of the Act of 1953, it is found that any other law including the Act of 1948 has no manner of application in the case of requisition and acquisition of any land by the then DIT at present RAJUK under the Act of 1953. By referring the entire Act of 1953 as well as the subsequent amendments as made up to date he submits that there are different modes for requisition and acquisition of the property by RAJUK as well as disposal of the same. So the Act of 1948 which is completely a separate law cannot be applicable in any case of acquisition or requisition under the Act of 1953 in any manner. He also referred subsection 3 of section 93A of 1953 and submits that immediately after requisition the property shall vest with the RAJUK. Lastly, he submits that the judgment of the High Court Division, upon which, the respondent No.7 relied is a judgment per in curium. In support of his contention he referred to the following reported cases: Managing Director, Rupali Bank vs Tafazal Hossain, 44 DLR (AD) 260, Sadeque Uddin Ahmed vs Jabed Ali, 3 MLR (AD) 91, Jamir Ali vs Secretary, Ministry of Land, 52 DLR 125, Jamir Ali vs Secretary, Ministry of Land, 52 DLR (AD) 176, Abdul Hoque vs Government, 9 MLR (AD) 151 = 9 BLC (AD) 56, Sadeque Uddin Ahmed, vs RAJUK, 46 DLR 205 and Al-liaj Abul Basher vs Bangladesh, 50 DLR (AD) 11. 

 7. Mr AQM Shafiullah, the learned Advocate along with Mr Abdun Nur appearing on behalf of the.RAJUK in their respective cases supported the contentions of the petitioners. By placing affidavit-in-opposition they supported the case of the petitioner in Writ Petition No.11817-11819 of 2006 and 3466 of 2007. Mr Shafiullah submits that without hearing the requiring body there is no scope to deal with any acquisitioned or requisitioned land by any other authority and in the instant case it appears that though RAJUK is the requiring body but Ministry of Land has released the land without notifying or hearing the RAJUK in any manner. In support of his contention he referred by the case reported in Bangladesh vs M/s Commercial Trust of Bangladesh, 14 BLD (AD) 72 = 46 DLR (AD) 89. He also submits that after acquisition and after payment of compensation the same reaches the finality of a process and after finality there is no scope to release, any land remains vacant or unutilized and such un utilization does not create any right in favour of any person to get back his/her land by way of right. In this respect he referred the case reported in Al-haj Abul Bather vs Bangladesh, 50 DLR (AD) 11. 

 8. Mr Md Rezaul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 7 submits that the Ministry of Land issued the impugned memo and notification in accordance with law and, as such, the same cannot be interfered by this Court. He submits that the Government namely the Ministry concerned enjoys ample authority to release any land either under requisition or acquisition and, as such, the respondent-Government committed no illegality in issuing the impugned memo as well as notifications. He further submits the High Court Division in writ petition No. 835 of 1977 has rightly set aside the entire LA case in question resulting the issuance of the impugned memo and notifications which requires no interference by this Court. 

 9. Perused the Writ Petitions, affidavits-in-opposition, provisions of law, decisions as referred to and heard the learned Advocates for the contesting parties. On perusal of the same it appears that a common question of law has been raised in all these Writ Petitions. It appears from the record that the then DIT at present RAJUK acquired certain portion of land for the development of Dhaka city and for the implementation of residential scheme in the area specified in the Town Improvement Act of 1953. The said process was initiated and completed as per the provisions laid down in the said Act of 1953. It appears that after completion of acquisition and payment of compensation, the requiring body decided to release some land which appears to be in communication stage in between the authorities. As per the papers submitted by the respondent No. 7, it appears that there are certain conditions stipulated at that time before releasing such properties and as the owners refuse to accept the conditions the authorities cancelled the proposal for release and challenging the same Writ Petition No. 835 of 1977 was filed and the Rule was made absolute and on the basis of the said judgment the impugned memo and notifications were made. 

 (4) Acquisition of requisitioned property— 

 (b) Such notice shall state particulars of the property to be acquired and shall require all persons interested in the property to appear personally or by agent before the Deputy Commissioner at a time and place therein mentioned (such time not being earlier than 15 days after the date of publication of the notice) and to state the nature of the respective interest in the property, the objections (if any) to the acquisition of the property and particulars of their claims, the compensation for their respective interest. 

 (e) Every person required to make or deliver a statement under sub-section (2), (3) and (4) shall be deemed to be legally bound to do so within the meaning of sections 175 and 276 of the Penal Code. 

 (g) The Government after considering the report made under clause (f) shall make a decision about the acquisition of the requisitioned property and such decision of the Government shall be final. 

 (i) For the purpose of enquiries in connection with the acquisition of a requisitioned property for the Board the Deputy Commissioner or an officer authorized by him shall have the power to summon and enforce the attendance of witnesses including the parties interested or any of them and to compel the production of documents by the same, and (so far as may be) in the same manner as is provided in the case of a Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 (b) (i) Where no such agreement can be reached, the Deputy Commissioner shall assess a compensation for the immovable property having regard to the provisions of sections 23, 24 and 24 24A, as modified by section 81 of this Act, and sub-section (2) of section 35 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, so far as the same can be made applicable, and he shall give immediate notice of the assessment to the person or persons interested: 

 (iii) The application shall state the grounds on which objection to assessment is taken: 

 (c) At the commencement of the proceedings before the Tribunal, the Board and the persons to be compensated shall state what in their respective opinion is a fair amount for compensation. 

 (2) The acquisition of any land or interest in land for the Karitipakkha this sections, or for any scheme under this Act, shall be deemed to be an acquisition for a public purpose within the meaning Of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 (II of 1982), and the provisions of the said Ordinance shall apply to all such proceedings." 

 15. On a plain reading of the aforesaid provisions of law, it appears that the Town Improvement Act, 1953 being a special law enacted for a very special and specific purpose and which is also a complete, law to deal with any land in any manner which included acquisition as well as disposal of the same and as per the said law the then DIT at 'present RAJUK is the ultimate authority in such cases. 

 16. Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 is the law incorporated in the year 1948 which is an ordinary legislation for the purpose of requisition of the property in connection with the administration and development of the new province, East Bengal and as per section 1(4) of the said Act, the said law namely Act of 1948 shall remain in force for a period of 34 years. As per the said provision of law the Act has been repealed on 16-8-1982 i.e. on the expiry of 34 years. Section 5 of the said law deals with the manner of acquisition of property whereas section 8 as well as 8B of the said Act deals with withdrawal from acquisition and requisition of the property. Section 8B of the said Act deals with the provision relating to withdrawal from acquisition which runs as follows: 

 8B. Withdrawal from Acquisition—When owner of any property which has been acquired under section 5 is willing to receive back the property, the Government may, at any time before the payment of compensation withdraw from the acquisition of any such property by notification published in the Official Gazette, and on such withdrawal, the property shall be restored to the possession of the owner, and with effect from the date of such restoration, the property shall vest back in the owner with the rights which he had before such property was acquired." 

 17. So it appears that the Act of 1948 is a separate legislation providing for the provisions for acquisition and requisition under the said law as well as the provisions of release of the same from acquisition or requisition. From the four corners of the said law namely Act of 1948 we do not find any provisions that the said law is applicable to any other law for the purpose of either acquisition and/or release of the same in any manner. In the case of Abdul Huq vs Government of the Peoples Republic of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary Ministry of Land, reported in 9 MLR (AD) 151 = 9 BLC (AD) 56, Their Lordships deals with the provisions of release of land acquired under the Town Improvement Act, 1953. Their Lordships observed as follows: 

 21. It appears that after the natural death of Act of 1948 on 16-8-1982 the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 came into force and in the said law certain provisions have been inserted which specifically attracts the Town Improvement Act of 1953. But it appears from section 47 of the said Ordinance that if any proceeding initiated before the enactment of the said Ordinance it shall not affect any provision of this law and those proceeding shall be governed as if the instant Ordinance has not been amended. In the case of Jamir Ali (Md) vs Secretary, Ministry of Land, reported in 52 DLR (AD) 176 their Lordships held: 

 "Claim for release of unutilized acquired land is not a vested right and nor failure of the requiring body to utilize the land acquired within 3 years from the date of acquisition in view of the decision of the Government for acquisition of land as contemplated under section 12 is not applicable to the facts of the instant cases which were started long before the Ordinance came into force in view of the provision of amended section 79 of the 1953 Act as not retrospectively can be read into section 12 of the 1982 Ordinance." 

 22. The High Court Division also, while passing the judgment in the same case, held that in spite of repeal of section 93A and 93B of the Act 1953 the pending acquisition of the disputed land shall be continued under the aforesaid provisions as if those provisions have not been repealed and the provisions of section 12 or other provisions of Acquisition and Requisition of Immoveable Property Ordinance, 1982 shall not be applicable to the acquisition proceedings started under section 93 A of the Act of 1953. It appears in the cases in hand that certain communications were stated regarding release of certain land in question. From the Writ Petitions as well as from the affidavits-in-opposition it appears that the requiring authorities issued certain letters to the Deputy Commissioner for taking certain steps and also the Deputy Commissioner intimating the requiring body about the course of action but such type of communication cannot be used or create any legal right in favour of any person to get back any land under acquisition. This view is taken by their Lordships in the Appellate Division in a case reported in Al-Haj Abul Basher vs Bangladesh, 50 DLR (AD) 11. It further appears that in the instant case the impugned notifications were issued by the Ministry of Land exercising the power conferred under section 8(b) of the Act of 1948 long after the natural death of the said Act. It also appears that before issuing such notification, no intimation of the impugned action has been made to the RAJUK who is the requiring body which is a sine-qua-non3 for issuing such notification for taking such step. This view is also supported by a decision reported in Bangladesh vs M/s Commercial Trust of Bangladesh, 14 BLD (AD) 72 = 46 DLR (AD) 89. 

 23. Section 8(b) of the Act of 1948 has been examined by our Apex Court in several occasions and their Lordships while examining the same consistently held that once compensation has been paid, it reaches it finality and, as such, there is no question of release of any land from acquisition. The decision reported in Md Matiur Rahman vs Bangladesh, 15 BLD 331 = 46 DLR 638 also supports this contention. In a case reported in Rangamati Food Products Ltd. vs Commissioner of Customs, 10 BLC 525 the High Court Division held that a decision of this Court is not binding if it is judgment per in curium. In the instant case the respondent No.7 resorted to the decision passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.835 of 1977. We have carefully" examined the entire judgment passed by their Lordships but it appears that at the time of hearing, no law either the Act of 1953 or Act of 1948 so far as it relates to acquisition and requisition has been referred therein in any manner. In the said judgment their Lordships only set aside the decision of a Joint Secretary of a Ministry so far as it relates to an observation that the RAJUK, the then DIT, may start a fresh process of acquisition. From the plain reading to the aforesaid judgment we do not find any single word to the effect that the High Court Division has cancelled the entire LA Case No. 10 of 1963-64. 

 28. From the Judgment of the High Court Division as well as the provisions of law it appears that the Ministry of Land is not the authority either in law or by the judgment passed by the High Court Division to issue such letter. It appears that the letter issued pursuant to the judgment is a misinterpreted one and based upon misconception of law. Taking any step by misinterpretation of the judgment of this Court, which is the integral part of the Constitution, tantamount to a serious disobedience to this Court and ultimately to the Constitution and creates serious bottleneck in the property adjudication of the administration of justice. Especially when such interpretation is coming from a respectable officer like Senior Assistant Secretary of the Ministry of Land which is the highest executive Office relating to land of the Country. It appears that in numerous decisions Their Lordships of our Apex Court time and again reminded that after finality there is no scope to release any land from acquisition especially after payment of compensation but it appears in the instant proceeding that time and again by violating the direction made by their Lordships in numerous decisions the Government functionaries are issuing different letters and notifications violating the settled principle of law which seriously affected the administrative function as well as violating the process of law and also violating the provisions of law concerned. 

 29. In the instant case it appears that though there is a procedure of release under the Act of 1953, the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 7 failed to show us any document so far as it relates to the final decision to de-requisition for the land in question by the authority concerned and it appears that such communication started in the years 1960 and notifications was issued in the year of 1990 to 2001 to long after 30 years. In the instant case the Act of 1948 has no manner of application in any manner in a case of Acquisition and requisition by the Town Improvement Act of 1953 but it appears that long after 30 years the impugned notifications were made by a different authority referring the Act of 1948. Under such circumstances we are of the view that the Ministry of hand should not be allowed further to issue such misconceived and arbitrary notifications which causes serious problems in the day to day affairs of land management.
